title: Functions and arguments
goals: Distinguish a function definition from a function call
Match positional arguments to parameters in order
Reuse one function and test that it uses the supplied values

prerequisite.prompt: A script sets capacity = 12 and used = 4. What does print(capacity - used) display?
prerequisite.answer: 8. Subtraction is ordered: reversing these values would produce -8.

vocabulary: A named block of reusable instructions that runs when called
Code that creates a function and specifies its body
An instruction that runs a function with supplied arguments
A name in a function definition that receives an argument
A value supplied when calling a function

lesson.title: Name a calculation you need again

blocks.text: A fictional supply cupboard records capacity and the number of occupied spaces. The remaining-space calculation is capacity minus used. Instead of copying the same instructions for every cupboard, define one function and call it with different values. A function makes a procedure reusable; its name alone does not guarantee that its instructions are correct.

Our input contract requires nonnegative integer counts with used no greater than capacity. The example assumes these conditions; it does not validate them. This week the function prints its result. Week 9 will show how to return a value for later calculations.

lesson.title: Define once and call with new values

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def show_remaining(capacity, used):
    remaining = capacity - used
    print(remaining)

show_remaining(12, 4)
show_remaining(10, 7)

blocks.title: Arguments matched in order
blocks.caption: Each call runs the same body with the values supplied for that call.

blocks.text: def introduces the definition. The function name is followed by parameter names in parentheses and a colon. Four-space indentation marks the body. Executing the definition creates the function but does not run its body. The two unindented calls then run it, producing 8 and 3 on separate lines. A blank line helps readability; indentation determines the block.

lesson.title: Trace the call before running it

rows: Create the function; no output yet

blocks.text: In show_remaining(12, 4), 12 and 4 are arguments; capacity and used are parameters. Positional arguments match from left to right. show_remaining(4, 12) produces -8, showing why order matters; it also violates our written input contract. Use a fresh file with the definition before its calls.

blocks.label: Predict the output of show_remaining(9, 9) followed by show_remaining(9, 0). Name the parameter receiving each argument. What would be printed if both calls were removed?

lesson.title: Check whether the function uses its arguments

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def show_remaining(capacity, used):
    remaining = 12 - 4
    print(remaining)

show_remaining(12, 4)
show_remaining(10, 7)

This faulty function prints 8 twice. Its fixed numbers ignore the arguments. Replace 12 - 4 with capacity - used, then rerun both calls. Testing only the first call would miss the bug because its expected answer happens to be 8.

For this two-parameter definition, show_remaining(12) raises TypeError because an argument is missing. Correct the call to supply both values. Naming a function without calling it does not execute the body: the parentheses in show_remaining(12, 4) are part of the call.

For each call, record the supplied arguments, expected printed output and observed output. Include different values that produce different answers, plus a valid zero-result case. Call order controls output order; it does not change the subtraction rule. These functions use supplied data and written instructions, not a pattern learned from examples.

blocks.label: A learner tests only show_remaining(12, 4) and says the function works for every cupboard. Give a second valid call that exposes the fixed-number bug, state its expected output and explain what passing two tests still cannot prove.

workbook.title: Label the parts
workbook.prompt: In def show_remaining(capacity, used), identify the function name and parameters. In show_remaining(15, 6), identify the arguments and their matching parameters.
workbook.answer: Name show_remaining; parameters capacity and used. Arguments 15 and 6 match capacity = 15 and used = 6. Expected printed result 9.

workbook.title: Follow the execution order
workbook.prompt: Using the correct definition, predict show_remaining(8, 3), show_remaining(8, 8) and show_remaining(8, 0) in that order. Explain what happens if the file contains only the definition.
workbook.answer: The calls print 5, 0 and 8 on separate lines. A definition alone creates the function but prints nothing because its body has not been called.

workbook.title: Repair ignored arguments
workbook.prompt: The faulty body calculates 12 - 4 regardless of the call. State the output and expected output for show_remaining(11, 2). Repair the expression and name an earlier call to rerun.
workbook.answer: Faulty output 8; expected 9. Use capacity - used. Rerun show_remaining(12, 4), expecting 8, as well as the revealing call.

workbook.title: Create a new function independently
workbook.prompt: Each sealed box contains 6 counters. Define show_stock(boxes, loose) to print the total counters using its two parameters. Assume nonnegative integer arguments. Call it with (3, 2), (0, 2) and (3, 0). Predict each output and explain why show_stock(2, 3) is a different case.
workbook.answer: The body prints boxes * 6 + loose. Outputs are 20, 2 and 18. show_stock(2, 3) gives 15 because boxes and loose have different roles. Define once and use three calls; do not hard-code one answer.

workbook.title: State the input assumption
workbook.prompt: The correct subtraction function prints -1 for show_remaining(4, 5). Does successful execution make this a valid cupboard record? Explain what the function assumes and what needs checking.
workbook.answer: No. used exceeds capacity and violates the contract. The function calculates with supplied values but does not check the contract. A separate validation check or guarded function is needed to reject invalid records.

teacher.background: Teach definition, call, parameter and positional argument as distinct ideas. Keep inputs scalar and avoid mutable-list aliasing in this first function lesson. Reference: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#defining-functions. These functions print results; reusable return values and local state are taught in Week 9.
materials: Parameter cards labelled capacity and used
Call cards and a table for expected and observed output
sessions: Retrieve ordered subtraction with the prerequisite.
Read the contract and label the definition and calls for W1.
Match argument cards to parameters and trace the worked calls.
Complete W2 and the guided question before running the file.
Retrieve why a definition alone prints nothing.
Run the fixed-number bug, complete W3 and rerun the earlier case after repair.
Collect the independent W4 function and predictions before hints.
Discuss W5 and use the exit to assess the limits of passing tests.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The calls print 0 then 9. capacity receives 9 in both calls; used receives 9 then 0. Removing both calls leaves a definition with no printed output. Exit: show_remaining(10, 7) should print 3 but the faulty version prints 8. Passing two cases does not establish correctness for all allowed inputs or validate the input contract.
misconceptions: Writing def runs the body immediately
The definition creates the function; a call runs its body.
Arguments and parameters are interchangeable labels
Parameters are names in the definition; arguments supply values at a call.
Different parameter roles can give different results when values are swapped.
A correct first example proves the function is reusable
Fixed numbers can match one case while ignoring later arguments.
teacher.assessment: W4 must define one function, use both parameters, call it three times and predict 20, 2, 18; the swapped case must give 15. After support, retry show_tiles(packs, singles) with 4 tiles per pack: calls (2, 3), (0, 3), (2, 0) print 11, 3, 8; swapped (3, 2) prints 14. Record assistance and collect new predictions before execution.
teacher.support: Use two labelled parameter spaces and place argument cards left to right. Permit an oral execution trace alongside code. Extension: add an if check inside show_remaining that prints Invalid when used exceeds capacity, otherwise prints the difference; test (4, 5) and (4, 4). This checks only that one constraint.
teacher.next: Week 9 returns results to the caller and explains local variables and fresh state on each call.
